messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: comment on stan manual
parts:
I'd love to see an example of linear regression with multiple predictors, y=Xb+error, in vector-matrix form. That is, an example where the predictors come in as a matrix and the coefficients are estimated as a vector, but just regular linear regression. I'm trying to write such a model, and the difficulty is that the first example with vector notation for b is in section 12.5, but then there's also a bunch of other things going on with softmax etc., so it's hard for me to figure out exactly what I need to do.

So I'll try to figure it out and write it up as a section in the Stan manual, I think it would go right in section 12.1, it doesn't really need a new section since it's not a new model.

So, since I am doing it, just a quick question: is there a way of doing such a model so that the likelihood can be written in a single line (without a loop)?

Also, this is just personal taste, but in that example in Section 12.5, is it really the best advice to give different lower bounds on K, N, and D in the data statements? I understand what you're doing: you need at least 2 outcomes, at least 0 data points, and at least 1 beta, but to me, as a user, I find all this a bit intimidating. A simple int K,N,D; would do the job just fine for me (or, if they have to be on separate lines: int K; int N; int D;). I understand the value of supplying info in the declaration, but I worry that a user will get tangled in these details and, if anything, I could see someone being _more_ likely to mess up because of screwing up somehow in the bounds in the declarations (for example, giving a lower bound of 2 on D). So in this (and similar) examples, I'd vote for not putting any bounds on the discrete parameters, with a note saying that there is a tradeoff: giving a correct bound is a debugging device and provides some information about the model, but the cost is that the declarations look more complicated and there is a chance of getting it wrong.

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] comment on stan manual
parts:
On 12/14/13, 2:43 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> So, since I am doing it, just a quick question: is there a way of doing such a model so that the likelihood can be
> written in a single line (without a loop)?

The yet-to-be-written FAQ should be pointing you to page 166/167
of the 2.0.1 manual. I think that has what you're looking for.

It probably makes sense to duplicate the model back in the
regression section because this is the obvious way to write
the model for users with even a basic comfort level with matrix
multiplication.

> ... So in this (and similar) examples, I'd vote for not putting any bounds on the
> discrete parameters,

This is just data --- there are no discrete parameters in Stan.
I'm not just being pedantic here. Data constraints are optional
and may (a) help with debugging, (b) help clarify the model, and/or (c)
confuse everyone (user and reader). Parameter constraints are also
optional, but if you don't include them, chances are sampling will be
either inefficient or not work at all.

> with a note saying that there is a tradeoff: giving a correct bound is a debugging device and
> provides some information about the model, but the cost is that the declarations look more complicated and there is a
> chance of getting it wrong.

Let's present this discussion in the manual and leave it
up to the users. It's more likely in my experience that users
will provide too lax a bound (or no bound at all as is your
preference). If they get tangled in the bound and make it too
strict, they'll find that out when they try to read in data.

I can present the model first your way and then with stricter
constraints.

The real issue's where to put all of these things, since we can't
expect users to read the whole manual.

- Bob
